Relaypad has no account system and no server of ours between you and your game console. Your gameplay, your console and your sign-in never pass through us.

  • What we do collect: anonymous usage events through Google Analytics for Firebase. They are on by default and you can switch them off in Settings → Privacy → Usage statistics. They never include your account ID, your IP address, your console's name, your stream keys or your channel names (§4).
  • Where else the app connects: your own console, the console manufacturer's sign-in and remote play services if you sign in, public STUN servers for remote connections, your router, Google Play and Firebase, the streaming platform you pick if you go live (§11), and, only if you set it up yourself, the AI provider whose API key you enter (§10). §2 lists every destination.
  • If you go live: the game's picture and sound, plus your microphone, camera and chat overlay only if you switched them on, go straight from your device to the streaming platform you chose. There is no relay server of ours in between, and we never see the stream, your stream key or your channel (§11).
  • What stays on your phone: pairing keys, sign-in tokens and stream keys, encrypted with a key that cannot leave the device, plus your consoles, settings and layouts (§3).
  • You can check this yourself: the permissions are visible in Android's Settings → Apps → Relaypad → Permissions and listed in §13, and the app's source code is public (§1).

About this policy

Relaypad is an independent, unofficial Android app that turns your phone into a controller for a game console and streams the console's picture to your device. It can also broadcast that picture live to a streaming platform you choose. This policy explains what happens to information when you use it.

It covers the Relaypad app as published on Google Play. It does not cover your console or the services run by its manufacturer, the streaming platforms you broadcast to, Google Play itself, your router, or any modified build of Relaypad distributed by someone else.

Relaypad is free software licensed under the AGPL-3.0, so the statements in this policy can be checked against its source code: codeberg.org/geektech54/gamec.

Questions, requests or complaints: feedback@dapplebyte.com.

Where your data can go

This is every destination the app sends data to, and what triggers each one. Nothing else leaves your device.

DestinationWhat it receives, and when
Your consoleDiscovery and wake-up broadcasts on your local network, pairing requests, controller input, microphone audio while the console microphone is on, and the video and audio stream coming back. This is a direct connection between your device and your console, either on your local network or through the manufacturer's remote play service when you play away from home. We are not part of it and never see it.
The console manufacturer's servicesOnly if you sign in. You sign in on the manufacturer's own web page, and the app then uses the resulting token with the manufacturer's services. §5 lists exactly what for.
A public account-ID lookup serviceOnly if this option is offered and you choose "look up by Online ID" during setup. It is hidden unless we switch it on remotely (§9) and is off by default; while it is off the app never contacts this service. When used: the Online ID you type is sent to psn.flipscreen.games, an independent third-party service, which returns the matching account ID. See §6.
Public STUN serversWhen you run the connection doctor, connect from outside your home network, or register a console without a pairing code: short packets to public STUN servers so the app can learn how your network translates addresses. These servers see the public IP address your connection comes from, the same thing any website sees. Nothing that identifies you is attached. See §7.
GitHubRarely: if the app's built-in STUN server list cannot be used for a remote connection, it downloads a public list of STUN servers from raw.githubusercontent.com. The request carries nothing that identifies you.
Your routerUPnP requests on your local network when the connection doctor runs, when a remote or code-free connection is set up (which may add a temporary port mapping), and when you use automatic port mapping. This stays inside your home network.
Google PlayWhen you buy the app, buy or restore Pro, rate the app, or open the store page of another app of ours from a suggestion. Google processes the payment; we never see your payment details. See §8 and §9.
Google Analytics for FirebaseAnonymous usage events, while the statistics switch in Settings is on. See §4.
Firebase Remote ConfigA request for our current configuration values, made when the app starts, including when statistics are switched off. See §9.
An AI provider you choose (optional)Only if you turn on the AI copilot and enter your own API key for Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek or an OpenAI-compatible service, and only when you ask for something: the game guide topic you typed, the game name, your follow-up questions with the current guide, a reduced screenshot of the stream if you chose to attach one or asked to have the screen described, and, for the guide search, the provider runs web searches on your behalf using those words. The request goes straight from your device to that provider under your own key and the provider's own terms; it never passes through us, and we keep no copy. Guides come back to your device and are stored there only. See §10.
The streaming platform you choose (only if you go live)The broadcast itself: the game's picture and sound and, only if you switched them on, your microphone, your camera picture and the chat overlay. It goes from your device straight to the platform's server at the address of the destination you set up, together with your stream key, which is how the platform knows whose channel it is. Testing a connection opens a short connection to the same server. We run no relay, and the stream does not pass through us. See §11.
Twitch (only if you sign in with Twitch)Requests to Twitch's sign-in service and API under the permission you gave: your user and channel details, your stream key, title and category, the viewer count, your channel's chat and events, and the chat messages and moderation actions you send from the app. See §11.
Google and YouTube (only if you sign in with YouTube)Sign-in through Google on your device, then requests to the YouTube Data API under the permission you gave: your channel, the live broadcast the app creates for you and its title, the viewer count and, where it is enabled, live chat. See §11.
Apps you chooseOnly when you tap to send feedback, share a screenshot, open or share a recording, share a connection-doctor report, or open a web page from the app (a platform's stream-key page, for example, opens in your browser): your email app, your browser or the app you pick receives it, and what happens next is up to you and that app. See §10.

What stays on your device

Relaypad keeps what it needs in Android's private storage for the app, which other apps cannot read. Uninstalling the app or using Android's Clear storage deletes all of it. The exceptions are stream screenshots and recordings, described below the table.

WhatDetails
Pairing keysThe registration keys your console issues when you pair. Encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a key held in the Android Keystore, which cannot be extracted from the device.
Sign-in tokens and device IDIf you signed in: the access and refresh tokens issued by the manufacturer, encrypted the same way. Also a random device identifier the app generates for remote play (§5). Removing the account in the app deletes the tokens.
Account detailsThe account ID your console needs before it will pair, your Online ID if known, and which sign-in method you used. Never sent to us, never attached to usage statistics.
Your consolesFor each console: the name you gave it, its local and MAC address, generation and firmware version, the console's own ID from the manufacturer, the console passcode if you entered one, whether Remote Play was enabled, the game or app it last reported running, and when you paired and last connected. This lets the app find, wake and reconnect to it.
Your settings and layoutsStream, controller, network and display preferences, controller layouts you create, button mappings for physical gamepads (with the gamepad's name), vibration strength, theme, the statistics switch, and small flags such as which tips you have already seen.
Purchase stateWhether Pro is unlocked, with the product ID, order ID and purchase time reported by Google Play, so the app works offline.
Streaming destinations and stream keysFor each destination you save: the platform, the name shown in the list (for a signed-in account, the channel name), the server address and whether it is landscape or portrait. The stream key is kept separately, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under the same Android Keystore key. Deleting a destination deletes its key.
Twitch and YouTube accountsIf you signed in with Twitch: your Twitch user ID, login name, display name, profile picture address and last stream title, plus the access and refresh tokens, which are encrypted the same way. If you signed in with YouTube: your channel ID and name, profile picture address, the IDs of the stream and broadcast the app created, the last title, and the email address of the Google account, which is encrypted. The app stores no YouTube token. Signing out deletes all of it (§11).
Live settingsYour layout, quality and sound choices for going live, any text you put on the broadcast layout such as scene cards, which destination you used last, the list of chat users you blocked on this device (platform and user ID only, no names or messages), whether you accepted the chat notice and turned on read-aloud, and how many trial broadcasts you have used.
CachesCookies and cache from the in-app sign-in page; a per-network note of whether your router supports UPnP and what the last address-translation test found, filed under a one-way hash of the network rather than its name or address; and the state of the home-screen widget.
Connection-doctor summaryOne line summarising the last run, kept so it can be included if you choose to send feedback.

Screenshots. If you take a screenshot during a stream, it is saved as a picture on your device: on Android 10 and newer in Pictures/Relaypad, where it stays after you uninstall the app; on Android 8 and 9 in the app's own folder, which is removed on uninstall. A temporary copy is kept in the app's cache so it can be shared.

Recordings and replays. If you record a session or save an instant replay, the video is saved on your device: on Android 10 and newer in Movies/Relaypad, where it stays after you uninstall the app; on Android 8 and 9, or if that folder cannot be written, in the app's own folder, which is removed on uninstall. A recording contains whatever was in the broadcast picture and sound, including your microphone, camera and chat overlay if they were on.

Backup and transfer. The app excludes all of its data from Android backup and from device-to-device transfer, so none of it is copied into your Google account's cloud backup or moved to a new phone when you set it up from an old one.

The cost of keeping keys on the device: pairing keys, sign-in tokens and stream keys cannot be restored to a new phone or recovered after a factory reset. On a new device you sign in, pair and enter your stream keys again. We cannot recover them for you, because we never had them.

Anonymous usage statistics

Relaypad uses Google Analytics for Firebase to count how features are used, so we can see which screens fail and which parts are worth improving. Statistics are on by default and can be switched off in Settings → Privacy → Usage statistics. Switching them off stops collection straight away and it stays off.

The events the app sends itself are a fixed set, defined in the source code:

  • the steps of the setup wizard and how each ended, which of the ways in §6 you used to get your account ID and whether it worked, whether pairing succeeded, and whether you paired with a code or through your account;
  • the play button on the home screen (which mode, and whether the connection started), switches between streaming, remote and controller modes, and, once per install, whether a console was found on your network (its generation only);
  • the start of a stream (local or remote), the arrival of its first picture, and how the session ended: a cause category, the kind of network route and a duration bracket;
  • once per install, a rough rating of whether your device is likely to handle streaming (a category, not the model);
  • changes to quality, controller and display settings;
  • paywall shown, purchase tapped, paywall closed, restore tapped, and the result of a purchase or restore (completed, pending, cancelled or failed);
  • FAQ opened, and which question was expanded;
  • remote connection attempts, the kind of route used (direct, around a VPN, through a proxy), the result of the pre-check, and how they ended;
  • external display detected, used or released;
  • the steps of the rating prompt (§9);
  • the first-run question and the suggestions for our other apps (§9): shown, which of the fixed answers you picked, tapped or dismissed;
  • the AI copilot: the entry shown, a key saved or tested (which provider), a request made, how long the answer took as a bracket, an error category, and which built-in voice command matched. Never the topic, the question, the guide or the picture;
  • going live: the Go Live button on the home screen, the setup opened, the platform picked (its fixed code from the built-in list, such as twitch or custom), a broadcast started (free, trial or Pro, the quality preset and the mode), failed (an error category), reconnected, or ended (a duration bracket and the reason); a recording started or ended (quality preset, duration bracket); and the live paywall shown.

Each event carries at most one short label, for example which entry point opened the paywall, which setting changed and its new value, or which failure category a sign-in, pairing or remote connection ended in. These labels never contain your account ID, your IP address, your console's name, the name of an external display, a stream key, a server address, a channel name, a stream title or anything from chat, and the app's analytics interface is built to keep it that way.

Google Analytics also records its own standard events, such as first open, app update and time spent in the app. Google attaches an app-instance identifier and standard device information: model, OS version, language, and an approximate country derived from your IP address. Google does not give us the IP address itself. We have removed the advertising-ID permissions that the analytics library would otherwise add, so no advertising identifier is collected. Events are kept for 14 months and then deleted.

Relaypad contains no advertising SDK, no attribution SDK and no crash-reporting SDK, and shows no third-party ads. The only promotion in the app is the suggestion of another app of ours described in §9.

Signing in for remote play

Remote play, and registering a console without a pairing code, require signing in to the console manufacturer's account. When you do:

  • the sign-in page is the manufacturer's own web page, opened inside the app or in your browser. We do not see, intercept or store what you type there;
  • the sign-in request includes a random device identifier that the app generates and keeps on your device, because the manufacturer ties remote play to the device that signed in;
  • the app exchanges the result for a token with the manufacturer's authentication service over HTTPS, and renews the token there when it expires, using the refresh token stored on your device;
  • the token is stored encrypted (§3) and used only with the manufacturer's services: to read your account ID, list the consoles on your account, register a console without a pairing code, check whether Remote Play is enabled on your console, and set up remote connections to your own console;
  • the token is never sent to us, and we have no server that could receive it.

What the manufacturer does with your account activity is governed by its own privacy policy, not this one. If you never sign in, none of this happens: you can still pair and play on your home network using an account ID obtained another way (§6).

If a proxy is in use. Where the manufacturer's online services are hard to reach, the app can send its requests to them, and the sign-in page, through a proxy. By default it follows the HTTP proxy your system or VPN app already announces, if there is one; in Settings you can turn this off or enter the address of a proxy yourself. The proxy belongs to you or your VPN app: we do not run or provide one. These requests stay encrypted with HTTPS on the way through it, and the game stream never goes through the proxy. If you tap the button that detects a local proxy, the app tries a few common ports on this device (127.0.0.1) and nothing leaves the device.

Getting your account ID

Your console only pairs with an app that presents your account ID. The app offers up to four ways to get it:

  • Sign in inside the app, on the manufacturer's page (§5);
  • Sign in in your browser and paste the resulting address back into the app (§5);
  • Type an account ID you already have. This is converted on your device and nothing is sent anywhere;
  • Look it up by Online ID, offered only for older consoles, and only while we have it switched on remotely (§9). It is off by default. When it is offered and you use it, the Online ID you type is sent to psn.flipscreen.games, a third-party service we do not run and are not affiliated with, which returns the account ID. Nothing else is sent, and the request carries nothing that identifies your device.

Network checks and remote connections

The connection doctor, and the app when it sets up a remote connection, examine your network so they can tell you why a connection fails. The analysis runs on your device.

  • Checks that stay on the device: network type and Wi-Fi band, whether a VPN is active (and, if it hides the underlying network, what that network is), Bluetooth and connected gamepads, whether your phone and console are on the same subnet, whether the console responds and how fast, the system's bandwidth estimate, whether your account is ready for remote play, and external display state.
  • Checks that use the network: whether Remote Play is enabled on your console, asked of the manufacturer's service if you are signed in; whether your router supports UPnP, and the public address it reports; and STUN tests that show how your network assigns external addresses, which is how the app tells a carrier-grade NAT apart from a normal home router.
  • STUN servers are public servers run by independent operators, currently Cloudflare, Google, Nextcloud, Xiaomi, Twilio, Syncthing, Bilibili and the Moonlight project. The list is built into the app and may change between versions. They see the public IP address of your connection, as any internet server would. We receive none of it.

Results are shown to you, and a one-line summary is kept on the device for the feedback email. They are not uploaded. If you share or copy the full report yourself (§10), note that it includes your console's name, local addresses and your public IP address.

Purchases

Whether you pay for Relaypad on Google Play or unlock Pro with an in-app purchase, the payment is processed by Google Play. Google handles the payment and tells the app whether you are entitled to Pro; we never receive or store your payment method, card details or billing address. The app caches the entitlement on your device (§3) so it keeps working offline.

Refunds follow Google Play's terms and the refund policy shown in the app. If you email us for a refund, the order number you include is used only to find and refund the purchase.

Remote configuration, the rating prompt and app suggestions

Firebase Remote Config fetches our current configuration, for example the free-tier quality limit, switches that let us turn off a feature if a console update breaks it, lists of hardware video decoders known to misbehave, a compatibility notice, whether the rating prompt is enabled, whether the Online ID lookup (§6) is offered, paywall options and the launch-price deadline, the list of streaming platforms with their server addresses and setup steps, the app identifiers Twitch and Google issued to us for sign-in, and switches for chat and other live features. The request carries a Firebase installation identifier and basic app and device information, such as app version and language, so that Google can deliver the right values. It is not linked to your account or your consoles, and because the app needs it to work properly, it is made even when usage statistics are switched off.

The rating prompt is Google Play's official in-app review card. Whether you rate, and what you write, is handled entirely by Google Play, and the app never sees it. Relaypad only keeps a few values on your device to decide whether to ask at all: how many controller sessions you have started (it takes two by default), whether a single stream has run long enough (five minutes by default; we can adjust both thresholds remotely), and how many times and when it last asked Google Play to show the card. It asks at most twice in the app's lifetime, with at least 60 days between asks.

Suggestions for our other apps. The first time you open Relaypad it asks what you have: a console, only a gamepad, or neither. If you have no console it points you to another app of ours that fits better, and the home screen keeps an "I don't have a console" option while no console is set up. So that it does not suggest an app you already have, Relaypad checks whether those two specific apps are installed; it cannot see any other app on your device. Nothing opens by itself: if you tap a suggestion, its Google Play page opens with a tag saying the visit came from Relaypad, which lets Google Play's reports count it and carries nothing that identifies you. Your answer is remembered on your device so the question is not asked again and, if usage statistics are on, counted as one of the fixed choices (§4).

Things you choose to send or share

The feedback email

If you tap "Send feedback", the app opens your email app with a message addressed to us and pre-filled with: app version; device model, manufacturer and codename; Android version, API level and ROM build; language; for each paired console, its generation, firmware version and the name you gave it; the one-line summary of your last connection-doctor run; your purchase status, with product ID, order ID and purchase date if you have bought Pro; and whether Google Play Billing is reachable.

Nothing is sent until you press send in your own email app, and you can edit or delete any of it first. If you send it, we receive it at feedback@dapplebyte.com and keep it only as long as needed to help you.

Screenshots, recordings and connection-doctor reports

You can share a stream screenshot or a recording, or share or copy a connection-doctor report, through Android's share sheet or clipboard. The report includes your console's name, the local addresses of your phone and console, and your public IP address. It goes only where you send it, and from then on the app you picked, not this policy, governs what happens to it.

AI copilot: game guides and screenshots you ask about

The AI copilot is off until you turn it on and enter your own API key for an AI provider (Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, or any OpenAI-compatible service you name). Nothing is sent to any AI provider before that, and there is no key of ours in the app.

Game guides. When you search for a guide in the panel on the stream screen, the app sends the topic you typed, the game name, and your preferred language directly to the provider you chose, and asks it to search the web and write a step-by-step guide. The web searches are run by that provider (Anthropic, Google or OpenAI run them on their own servers; DeepSeek through its Anthropic-compatible endpoint), using your topic words as search terms, under the provider's own terms; a self-hosted or third-party OpenAI-compatible endpoint gets no web search and answers from the model alone. Follow-up questions send the current guide and your recent follow-ups along with the new question, so the provider has the context. If you tick Attach current screen, one reduced screenshot of the stream taken at that moment is included. Finished guides, your follow-ups and which steps you ticked are stored on your device only (at most 50 guides, deletable one by one or all at once in Settings); nothing is uploaded to us.

Describe the screen. When you ask for the screen to be described, by voice or from the quick panel, the app takes a reduced screenshot of the stream at that moment (up to two frames, so the provider can see what just changed) and sends it, with the name of the running game if your console reported it, directly to the provider you chose. There is no sampling in the background: pictures leave your device only when you ask. The provider processes every request under its own privacy policy and bills your own account; we are not part of that connection, do not receive the pictures, guides or answers, and keep no record of them. The app keeps only a count of requests and searches and an estimated cost for the current month, on your device.

Your API key is encrypted with a key held in the device's hardware key store, is excluded from backups, and is deleted immediately when you clear it. You can turn the whole feature off in Settings → AI copilot.

Live streaming

Relaypad can broadcast your session live to a streaming platform. Nothing in this section happens unless you set up a destination and go live yourself.

What is sent, and where

While you are live, the app builds the broadcast on your device and sends it directly to the platform you chose. There is no relay server of ours in between: we do not receive the stream, cannot watch it and keep no copy.

  • Always in the broadcast: the game's picture and the game's sound, and whatever you put on the layout yourself, such as a scene card. The privacy cover hides the game picture and mutes the sound in the broadcast while it is on, for moments like typing a password.
  • Only if you switch it on: your microphone, your camera picture, the chat overlay and on-screen alerts. Each has its own switch and all of them start off.

The built-in list of platforms is Twitch, YouTube, Kick, TikTok LIVE, Facebook, Instagram, X, Rumble, Telegram, Bilibili, Huya, Douyu, WeChat Channels, TwitCasting, niconico, SOOP, CHZZK, VK Video Live, Restream and Castr, and you can enter the address of any other RTMP server. We can update the list remotely (§9).

What a platform does with your broadcast, your account and your viewers is governed by that platform's terms and privacy policy, not this one. A live broadcast is public by nature: anything in its picture or sound can be seen, recorded and passed on by the people watching.

Encryption depends on the address. A server address that starts with rtmps:// is encrypted in transit. One that starts with rtmp:// is not: the broadcast and the stream key travel unencrypted and can be read by whoever runs the networks in between. At the time of writing the addresses built into the app for Twitch, YouTube, Kick and Facebook use rtmps://, the ones for Bilibili, SOOP, CHZZK and Restream use rtmp://, and for the other platforms it depends on the address the platform gives you.

Stream keys and destinations

A stream key is the password to your channel. You paste it, scan it, or, for Twitch and YouTube, let the app fetch it after you sign in. Keys you enter are stored encrypted on your device (§3) and are sent only to the server of that destination, when you go live or test the connection. They are never sent to us, and the app keeps them out of its usage statistics and its logs.

Testing a connection opens a connection to the destination's server and closes it again without broadcasting. For most platforms the key is not sent during the test. Twitch is the exception: the app uses Twitch's own bandwidth-test mode, which does send your key to Twitch's server so Twitch can confirm it, without putting you live.

Scanning a QR code. The scanner is provided by Google Play services and runs on your device. Relaypad does not use the camera permission for it and receives only the text of the code, which it puts into the form for you to check. The helper page at dapplebyte.com/key, which turns an address and key into a QR code on your computer, does its work inside your browser tab: what you type there is not sent anywhere and is not stored.

The clipboard. To save you typing, the step where you enter a key looks at the clipboard at three moments: when you reach that step, when you come back to the app after opening the platform's page from it, and when you tap Paste. If the text there looks like a stream address or key, the app asks whether to use it. It fills nothing in by itself, ignores anything else, and does not store or send what it read. Android may show its own notice that the clipboard was read.

Opening a platform's page. Links to a platform's stream-key page, help page or report page open in your browser, not inside the app, so the app does not see what you do there.

Signing in with Twitch

Instead of pasting a key you can connect your Twitch account. The app shows a code, you approve it on Twitch's own page in your browser, and Twitch gives the app a token. We never see your Twitch password, and no server of ours is involved: the app talks to Twitch directly.

The app asks Twitch for permission to:

  • read your stream key, so you do not have to copy it, and read and change your stream's title and category;
  • read your channel's chat and send messages to it as you;
  • delete chat messages and time out or ban users in your channel, when you choose to from the app;
  • see new followers, subscriptions and Bits, so they can be shown as alerts.

With that permission it reads your Twitch user ID, login name, display name and profile picture address, your channel's title and category, the stream key, and the viewer count while you are live. It keeps on your device the items listed in §3. The tokens are encrypted, and the stream key is not stored at all: the app asks Twitch for it each time you go live. None of this is sent to us or to anyone other than Twitch.

Signing out on the Destinations screen asks Twitch to revoke the token and deletes the account, its tokens and its destination from your device. You can also disconnect Relaypad on Twitch's side at any time, under Settings → Connections on twitch.tv.

Signing in with YouTube

Relaypad uses YouTube API Services for this feature. If you connect a YouTube channel, you sign in on Google's own account screen on your device, and we never see your Google password. By using this feature you agree to be bound by the YouTube Terms of Service. Google's handling of your data is described in the Google Privacy Policy.

The app asks for two permissions: to manage your YouTube account, which is the permission YouTube requires for creating a live broadcast, and to see the email address of the Google account, which is used only to remember which Google account the channel belongs to.

What the app reads through the API: the Google account's email address; your channel's ID, name and profile picture address; the live streams and broadcasts on your channel that it needs to reuse, including the stream's server address and stream key; and the viewer count while you are live.

What the app does on your channel: when you go live it creates a reusable live stream named "Relaypad" if there is not one already, creates a broadcast with the title you typed, links the two, and updates the title if you change it. The broadcast is created as public, starts when the app starts sending and ends when it stops. Afterwards YouTube normally keeps it on your channel as a video, as it does for any live stream, and you manage or delete it on YouTube. The app does not read your other videos, playlists, subscriptions, comments or watch history, and does not upload, edit or delete videos.

Live chat. Reading and moderating YouTube live chat from the app is switched off at present. If we enable it (§9), the app will read the chat of your own broadcast and, when you choose to, post a message, delete a message or ban a user in that chat, under the same permission.

What is stored, and who gets it: only the items listed in §3, only on your device. The Google account's email address is encrypted. The app stores no YouTube access or refresh token; it asks Google Play services for a short-lived token when it needs one and holds it in memory. Information obtained through YouTube API Services is not sent to us, sold, used for advertising or shared with anyone. It moves only between your device and Google.

Relaypad's use and transfer of information received from Google APIs to any other app will adhere to the Google API Services User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements.

Removing access and deleting the data. Sign out on the Destinations screen deletes the channel, its destination and the stored details from your device and, when no other channel from the same Google account remains, withdraws the app's access to that Google account. You can also revoke Relaypad's access yourself at any time on Google's security settings page, security.google.com/settings/security/permissions. Uninstalling the app or clearing its storage deletes everything it stored. For anything else, write to feedback@dapplebyte.com.

Chat and alerts

For a signed-in account whose platform supports it (Twitch at present), the app can show your channel's chat and events while you are live. Chat messages carry your viewers' display names and what they wrote. The app holds only the most recent messages, up to 200, in memory while you are live so it can display them. It does not write chat to storage, to logs or to usage statistics, and does not send it anywhere.

  • Messages you send, and the deletions, time-outs and bans you apply from the app, go to the platform under your account.
  • Blocking someone on this device hides their messages in the app only. So that the block lasts, the app remembers the platform and that user's ID on your device, not their name or messages.
  • If you turn on the chat overlay or alerts, the messages and events shown become part of the broadcast picture, and of any recording.
  • If you turn on read-aloud, messages are spoken by Android's text-to-speech engine on your device. The speech is played to you and is not mixed into the broadcast, although your microphone can pick it up if you are not using headphones. Which engine is used, and whether it works offline, depends on your device.

Camera and live microphone

The camera is used only to show you inside a broadcast or recording. Android asks for the camera permission the first time you switch it on. The camera picture goes into the broadcast frame and nowhere else; it is not stored separately and is never sent to us.

The live microphone is separate from the console voice chat in §12 and has its own switch, which starts off. While it is on, your voice is mixed with the game's sound and becomes part of the broadcast, of any recording and of the replay buffer. The app mutes it during a phone call.

Recordings and instant replay

Recording and instant replay save video to your own device only; §3 says where. Instant replay keeps about the last 30 seconds in memory while it is on and writes a file only when you save a clip. Nothing is uploaded, and a recording leaves the app only if you open or share it yourself (§10).

Microphone and voice

Relaypad can forward your microphone to the console, the same way a headset does, so you can talk in a game. Audio is captured only while you have that microphone turned on during a session and is sent directly to your console. On this path it is never recorded, stored or uploaded. Android asks for the microphone permission the first time you use it, and denying it only disables the features that need it.

The live microphone, which adds your voice to a broadcast or a recording, is a separate switch and is described in §11.

If you use the AI copilot's voice button, your speech is turned into text by Android's own speech recognition service while you hold the button; forwarding to the console pauses for that moment. On most devices the recognizer runs on the device; where it does not, the device's speech service (typically Google's) handles the audio under its own policy. The resulting text is matched against the voice-command list on your device; if it is not a command it goes to the game guide panel: as a topic for you to confirm when no guide is open, or as a follow-up sent, as text, to the AI provider you chose when a guide is open (§10). The app never records or stores the audio. Spoken answers use Android's text-to-speech on the device.

Relaypad requests no location, contacts, calendar, SMS, call-log, photo or file permissions, and does not read the list of apps installed on your device. It can only check whether two specific apps of ours are installed (§9).

Google Play

Separately from anything the app does, Google Play gives every developer aggregate statistics about their app's installs, uninstalls, ratings and crashes (Android vitals). Google produces these figures; the app does not send them to us, and they do not identify you.

Children

Relaypad is a utility for people who own a game console and is not directed to children under 13. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children. The app has no account system of its own and no third-party advertising. It has no chat or community of its own either: if you go live, the audience, the chat and any age rules are those of the streaming platform you chose, and what you broadcast is your own content under that platform's rules. If you believe a child has sent us personal information through the feedback email, write to us and we will delete it.

Your choices and your rights

  • Switch off statistics: Settings → Privacy → Usage statistics. Takes effect straight away and stays off.
  • Remove a console: Settings → Consoles → choose the console → Forget this console. This deletes its pairing keys and record from your device.
  • Remove an account: Settings → Accounts → Remove. This deletes the stored sign-in tokens and account details from your device.
  • Remove a streaming destination: delete it on the Destinations screen. Its stream key is deleted from your device with it.
  • Disconnect Twitch or YouTube: Sign out on the Destinations screen (§11). You can also revoke the app's access on the platform's side: Settings → Connections on twitch.tv, or Google's security settings page.
  • Delete everything: uninstall the app, or use Android's Clear storage. Nothing of yours is stored on a server of ours, so this removes all of it except the screenshots and recordings saved to your Pictures and Movies folders, which you can delete like any other file. Broadcasts and videos on a streaming platform are managed and deleted on that platform. There is no account of ours to delete.
  • Ask us: if you are in the EU/EEA, the UK, California or anywhere with similar law, you may ask what we hold about you, ask for a copy, or ask for deletion. In practice the only thing we can hold is an email you chose to send us. Write to feedback@dapplebyte.com and we will reply within 30 days.
  • Google's own controls: for the analytics and configuration data Google processes, see Google's privacy policy.

We do not sell or share personal information, and we do not use it for cross-context behavioural advertising. Relaypad shows no third-party advertising.

Legal basis, retention and transfers

Where the GDPR applies, our legal bases are: performance of our agreement with you for the features you ask for (pairing, streaming, remote play, going live and signing in to a streaming platform, purchases); our legitimate interest in keeping the app working and in telling you about a better-fitting app of ours, for Remote Config, the network checks described in §7 and the suggestions described in §9; and your consent for usage statistics, which you can withdraw at any time with the switch in Settings.

Retention: data on your device stays until you delete it or uninstall the app; usage events are kept by Google for 14 months; emails you send us are kept only as long as needed to help you. A broadcast you made is kept by the streaming platform under its own rules, not by us.

Google processes analytics and configuration data on servers that may be outside your country, under its own data-transfer safeguards. The streaming platform you broadcast to, and the AI provider you choose, do the same with what you send them. We run no servers of our own.

Security

Pairing keys, sign-in tokens and stream keys are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key held in the Android Keystore. Everything else the app stores, including channel names and server addresses, is protected by Android's app sandbox. Connections to the manufacturer's services, the lookup service, Twitch and Google are encrypted with TLS, and the stream between your device and your console is encrypted by the console's remote play protocol. A live broadcast is encrypted on its way to the platform only when the destination's address starts with rtmps:// (§11). No method of storage or transmission is perfect, but there is no central database of users to breach, because there is no server of ours.

Changes to this policy

If we change what the app does with data, we update this page and the effective date at the top. Material changes are also mentioned in the app's release notes on Google Play. The current version of this policy is always the one at this address.
